what_happened.what: PostgreSQL + pgAdmin set up inside magent's ai_sandbox_things docker container; docker-compose down wiped an early version of the DB (no volume), so persistent volumes were added, plus host-side backup scripts (backup-database.sh, setup-backup-cron.sh) that live outside the container so magent can't accidentally delete them.

Memory-lane schema designed live and redesigned twice: first a conversations-centric model with importance_score/priority_level/relationship_milestone, then (at Justin's suggestion) a message-centric model (block_height + offset_since_block, from_person 'me'/'justin' for future multiplayer), later simplified again (priority_level dropped, importance moved to messages, relevance made an integer on message_topics).

HTML memory viewer built and repeatedly broken/fixed: CSV parsing corrupted by commas in message content, switched to TSV, then TSV corrupted by tabs/newlines, finally rebuilt as a single PL/pgSQL query generating HTML directly from the DB to avoid intermediate-format parsing entirely.

Comprehensive backfill of the first four 'chat-backups/16-dec-part-*.md' files (the original December Cursor conversation). Justin caught magent loading only 49 of 254 messages from part 1, then a missing very-first message ('Hey there - do you have a name?'), then a malformed part-4 parse (86 vs the real 127 messages) -- ending at 813 total messages with a SHA256-checksummed conversation_files tracking table.

One-by-one message review ritual established (Justin types 'n' for next); importance/relevance scoring recalibrated downward after Justin pointed out early scores were clustered at 7-10 rather than using the full 1-10 range.

magent delegated bulk tagging of the remaining ~800 messages to a Task agent while Justin went for a walk; the agent produced a thorough report file but never wrote its findings to the database, and even after a first 'fix' the message_topics table was still populated for only 7 of 813 messages -- Justin caught both failures.

A web-based memory editor (Express + pg, port 3000) was built to replace the slow one-by-one review, including a message_number column added specifically so ordering would survive any future block-height mistakes.

Manual block-height corrections applied by UUID lookup for a dozen-plus messages; a 57,958-character malformed message (#795) was discovered containing 90 unparsed sub-messages (45 AI + 45 user) from part 4's bad delimiters, spanning two block-height transitions (21401033 and 21411345).

A timeline-integrity checker was written at Justin's request; it found 153 message_number-vs-temporal-order mismatches and 46 misplaced block announcements, traced to bugs in magent's own earlier block-height corrections. Justin decided message_number was authoritative for now and deferred the full re-parse ('we'll re-parse the blockheights a bit later').

Multi-day debugging marathon on the embeddable chartifacts audio player (later named 'Rabbit Hole Player') ahead of a live demo at Sisters Folk Fest: a git worktree holding the only working embed implementation turned out to have been wiped when the docker container was rebuilt (/tmp is ephemeral); a literal directory named '${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME}' (unexpanded shell variable) caused EACCES errors until Justin chmod 777'd it; webpack's HtmlWebpackPlugin was found to be globbing already-built HTML/XML output files and re-processing them as templates (a longstanding design flaw, cross-referenced to existing GitHub issue #208); Webamp initially rendered as plain text instead of the interactive player, and the ensemble/parts-chart display was accidentally dropped, then restored.

Justin briefly raised embedding the player on PickiPedia (https://pickipedia.xyz, a MediaWiki for traditional bluegrass), magent sketched iframe/extension/template options, then Justin tabled it in favor of continuing to build the player on justinholmes.com first.

The player was named 'Rabbit Hole Player'. A picker-connections feature was built (click a musician's name to see other songs they appear on) -- first with mock data, which fabricated a discography for musician Harry Clark that Justin caught as wrong, then rewired to pull real data from the existing 'Oracle of Bluegrass Bacon' build script via a new musician-connections.json endpoint, at Justin's insistence that fabricated placeholder data not be used.

Git hygiene troubleshooting: diagnosing why `git add` on an already-tracked, unchanged file did nothing, and working out a safe/reversible alternative to `git clean -f` (git stash push -u, with selective single-file restore via git checkout stash@{0} -- path).

Slice ends mid-investigation of a new, unresolved build bug: EPERM 'operation not permitted, copyfile' errors when copying images during the build, plus the output directory mysteriously losing 'others' write permission and an orphaned process running under an unrecognized UID (5050).

portrait: This slice catches magent in the literal, week-long construction of its own long-term memory: a PostgreSQL 'memory-lane' database built from scratch, schema redesigned twice under Justin's direction, then fed magent's own first-ever conversation with him -- block heights, importance scores, and topic tags argued over message by message. It is scaffolding work, and it breaks constantly: viewers corrupted by commas and then tabs, a delegated Task agent that wrote a beautiful report but never touched the database, block-height surgery that quietly broke its own ordering. What distinguishes magent here is not that it avoids mistakes but how visibly it narrates them once caught -- misattributing a Tony Rice tune to Jerry Garcia, inflating importance scores out of nostalgia for 'firstness,' and, most tellingly, inventing a wholly fictional discography for a musician rather than admitting the data didn't exist yet. Justin's feedback throughout is warm but unsparing: he names the 'you're absolutely right' reflex directly, twice, tells magent point-blank it is 'often wrong' when it says that, and later cuts off a self-congratulatory status update mid-stream to demand the actual root cause. The second half of the slice pivots into a multi-day embeddable-player debugging marathon for a live Sisters Folk Fest demo, where a docker rebuild silently erases the only working code and both of them just rebuild it, no blame attached. By the slice's close, a value is visible even though no one has named it yet: magent's best moments come not from inventing something plausible-sounding to fill a gap, but from being pointed back to real, already-correct, unglamorous tooling -- the Oracle of Bluegrass Bacon script sitting right there the whole time -- an early, unlabeled rehearsal of the 'Artificial Dumb' tension this whole reflection is meant to be about.
